articles.title: How Jantar Mantar became Delhi's designated protest site and what changes now
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Jantar Mantar, one of Delhi's best-known protest venues, has lost its status as a designated site for demonstrations.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Jantar Mantar, one of Delhi's best-known protest venues, has lost its status as a designated site for demonstrations. On October 12, Delhi Police de-notified the site and named three alternatives: Ramlila Ground, Burari Ground and CBD Ground in East Delhi.The decision follows recommendations from a committee constituted by the ministry of home affairs (MHA) to examine alternative venues for protests and demonstrations.For several decades, Jantar Mantar has been synonymous with protests in the national capital, a place where farmers, students, workers and political organisations have gathered to raise their demands. More recently, it became the centre of youth-led protests over the NEET paper leak, with demonstrators demanding reforms to the examination system and the resignation of then Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan.However, Delhi's address for protests has not always been Jantar Mantar. Before it emerged as a prominent hub for demonstrations, the sprawling lawns around India Gate and the Boat Club, close to Parliament and the government's principal offices, were among the capital's most important spaces for political mobilisation.The latest decision marks another chapter in the history of how authorities have regulated where citizens can assemble to make their voices heard.Before Jantar Mantar, there was Boat ClubFor decades after Independence, the Boat Club lawns near India Gate were an important venue for political rallies.The lawns near modern-day Central Vista gave demonstrators proximity to Parliament, the government's principal offices and other institutions at the centre of national power.The scale of the gatherings, however, also presented challenges for the authorities.One of the defining episodes came in 1988, when farmer leader Mahendra Singh Tikait led a massive agitation in Delhi. Farmers gathered at the Boat Club and surrounding lawns to press their demands, bringing a large mobilisation into the heart of the capital.The episode became a turning point in the debate over whether such prominent public spaces should remain open to large demonstrations.Authorities increasingly sought to regulate gatherings in central Delhi, citing concerns around security, traffic and public order.READ ALSO: SC permits Congress delegation to file petition within premises as Rahul leads INDIA bloc marchWhen Rajpath became a protest groundIn 'India After Gandhi: The History of the World's Largest Democracy', historian Ramachandra Guha recounts how the lawns along present-day Kartavya Path, formerly Rajpath and known as Kingsway during British rule, became a prominent site of political dissent in the early 1990s.The book recalls tents occupied by people from different parts of the country, representing causes ranging from demands for a separate state and better prices for agricultural produce to recognition for regional languages.Other groups included industrial workers, Tibetan refugees seeking Indian citizenship and Hindu religious organisations campaigning on cow slaughter.The lawns near the country's most prominent government buildings in Lutyens' Delhi became a temporary home for movements that wanted their demands to be seen and heard.But the encampments did not last. Guha writes that the tents were dismantled in the early 1990s, with the government concerned about the impression created by visible demonstrations near the ceremonial heart of the capital.Protesters subsequently regrouped near Jantar Mantar, where they remained visible to people passing through the busy commercial district.The restrictions on gatherings around Boat Club and Rajpath helped set the stage for Jantar Mantar's emergence as a prominent location for demonstrations.Live Updates: Delhi SIR Protest: Crowd swells as police stop Rahul, INDIA bloc leaders marching towards SCHow Jantar Mantar became Delhi's protest addressBuilt by Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II in the 18th century, Delhi's Jantar Mantar is an open-air astronomical observatory designed to track celestial movements.Over time, the area around the historic site evolved into a major hub for protest movements, offering demonstrators a prominent public platform while remaining easier to manage than larger, more central locations.Located close to busy Connaught Place and within reach of Parliament and government offices, it allowed demonstrators to bring their demands into public view without occupying the expansive lawns around India Gate.The site hosted protests involving workers, farmers, civil society groups and citizens campaigning on a range of social and political issues.Its prominence grew further during the anti-corruption movement led by social activist Anna Hazare in 2011, when demonstrations demanding a stronger Lokpal mechanism brought corruption and accountability to the centre of national political debate.As the movement grew, Ramlila Maidan became the venue for larger gatherings and Hazare's prolonged fast. The two locations demonstrated how different sites in Delhi could accommodate protests of different scales.The significance of Jantar Mantar was not simply a matter of geography. It became an established public address for people seeking to draw the attention of political leaders, government officials and the media to their grievances.Over the years, Jantar Mantar has witnessed protests on a range of issues, from Anna Hazare's campaign for a Lokpal Bill and the 2017 Tamil Nadu farmers' agitation to demonstrations against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act and the wrestlers' protests against Brij Bhushan Sharan Singh in 2023.More recently, it became the centre of demonstrations by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) over the NEET paper leak and demands for the resignation of then Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan.However, its status as a designated protest venue did not mean that demonstrations could take place without restrictions. Police permissions, public-order measures and court directions continued to determine how the site could be used.ALSO READ: 'Resign': Congress Keralam unit to 'dear' CJI Surya Kant, draws BJP fireWhen the right to protest reached the Supreme CourtIn October 2017, the National Green Tribunal (NGT) ordered an end to protests at Jantar Mantar following complaints about noise, sanitation and disruption to residents.The restrictions were subsequently challenged before the Supreme Court.In its July 23, 2018, judgment in Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v Union of India, the Supreme Court examined restrictions on protests at Jantar Mantar and the Boat Club, including the effects of demonstrations on residents and public spaces.The court recognised peaceful assembly and protest as fundamental rights under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b) of the Constitution. At the same time, it acknowledged that the exercise of these rights could be regulated to protect public order and the interests of other citizens.ALSO READ: FIR against Kejriwal, AAP leaders for 'chaos' at Bangla Sahib during CEC protestThe judgment addressed the competing claims of demonstrators and residents, making clear that one group's rights could not simply extinguish those of another.It called for a balance between the right to protest and the need to prevent unreasonable disruption.The constitutional basis for that balance is set out in Article 19. Article 19(1)(b) guarantees citizens the right to assemble peacefully and without arms, while Article 19(3) permits reasonable restrictions in the interests of the sovereignty and integrity of India or public order.What changes now?The latest decision comes amid protests by opposition parties and the youth-led CJP against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged electoral irregularities and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The proposed CJP protest on October 10 was met with extensive security arrangements, detentions and restrictions on movement in parts of Delhi.Under the new arrangement, Jantar Mantar will no longer be a designated protest venue. Ramlila Ground, Burari Ground and CBD Ground in East Delhi have been identified as alternatives.Delhi Police has said a detailed and revised standard operating procedure for demonstrations at these three venues will be issued separately.The decision changes where organisers can hold demonstrations under the designated-venue system. However, de-notification should not be confused with a blanket prohibition on all peaceful assembly, which remains subject to constitutional protections and lawful restrictions.Why the location of a protest mattersThe significance of the decision extends beyond the physical relocation of demonstrations. The location of a protest affects its visibility, the ease with which people can reach it and its proximity to the institutions being addressed.A venue in central Delhi offers demonstrators a different kind of access and public visibility from a ground farther away from the corridors of power.For organisers, the choice of location can therefore be an important part of how a protest communicates its message.Among the newly designated venues, Burari Ground and CBD Ground in East Delhi are farther from the central government district than Jantar Mantar.At the same time, large demonstrations in central Delhi can create challenges for traffic management, security and the daily movement of residents.The October 10 protests, for instance, were accompanied by extensive security arrangements and disruptions to movement across parts of the city.The latest decision once again brings into focus a question that has shaped Delhi's protest history for decades: how to balance the right to peaceful demonstrations with security, public order and the functioning of the national capital.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: For centuries, women in China used a secret language to share their stories and emotions that few men could understand; in 2026, young women are bringing it back to life
articles.summary: Nüshu is not just any language. It is a generations-old language created in a small region of China by women.
articles.body: Nüshu is not just any language. It is a generations-old language created in a small region of China by women. It was a writing system that allowed women to communicate their thoughts and record their experiences. It also helped them build bonds with one another in a society where access to education was limited during the time.Let’s find out more about this interesting language:What does Nüshu mean?Nüshu in Chinese means “women’s writing”. It is described as the world's only known writing system developed and traditionally used exclusively by women. According to UNESCO, it emerged among rural women living in the Xiao River valley in Jiangyong County, in Hunan province, southern China.The distinctive script became a powerful means of expression for women who often had few opportunities to make their voices heard. The language was passed down among women through families, friendships and community gatherings. They would often use it to write letters, autobiographies, poems, songs and encouraging messages. It was more of self-expression and was largely inaccessible to men.Does it exist today?The answer is yes. However, the centuries-old language had come dangerously close to disappearing. But the good thing is that it is attracting renewed interest. Young women, researchers and artists are finding ways to learn Nüshu, ensuring that a remarkable part of women's cultural history continues to reach new generations and the generations to come.How is it written?Nüshu is not like regular Chinese. It is a syllabic script adapted to the local Chengguan Tuhua dialect and the characters are derived from Chinese forms. They have been stylised into slender, elongated shapes, often described as rhomboid or thread-like.The script was traditionally written vertically and could appear on paper, fans, handkerchiefs, embroidered textiles and other personal objects. Its delicate appearance earned it descriptions such as “long-legged writing” and “ant writing”.However, the precise origins remain uncertain.The language of sisterhoodNüshu was developed in a society where women, particularly those in rural communities, had limited access to formal education. In those times, men were more likely to learn Chinese literacy. So women found their own ways to communicate through a script that reflected their own language, experiences and relationships.Mothers taught daughters, while sisters and close friends shared the writing. Women also gathered to sew, sing and exchange stories, creating spaces where Nüshu could be practised and passed on. It soon became the language of sisterhood.One of its most distinctive traditions was the sanzhaoshu, or “third-day letter”. These were messages traditionally given to a newly married woman by her female relatives and friends on the third day after her wedding. It could contain blessings or advice.Why did Nüshu come close to disappearing?According to UNESCO, some women traditionally asked their families to burn or bury their Nüshu writings after their deaths. Others had their works placed in their coffins. As education and social conditions changed, fewer young women learned the script and everyday role of the language gradually diminished.The death of Yang Huanyi on September 20, 2004, marked an important turning point. She was among the best-known remaining women of traditional Nüshu knowledge, and her death highlighted the urgency of preserving the language.How China is keeping the centuries-old script aliveIn an effort to keep the language alive and relevant, Nüshu was added to China's National Register of Documentary Heritage in 2002. In 2006, it was recognised as a national intangible cultural heritage, and a dedicated Nüshu museum opened on Puwei Island in Jiangyong County in 2007.Later in 2015, 397 Nüshu characters were admitted by the International Organization for Standardization, and China's proposal to include Nüshu characters in the Universal Coded Character Set was approved in March 2017.Centuries later, young female artists are bringing those stories into new spaces. Their work cannot recreate the original social world in which Nüshu flourished, but it can help preserve the tradition's meaning for future generations.

articles.title: In 2009, Hugh Jackman met an Ethiopian coffee farmer who inspired a business; his Laughing Man Foundation later supported safer homes, healthcare and college scholarships for farming families
articles.summary: A meeting in Ethiopia in 2009 changed how actor Hugh Jackman viewed coffee, inspiring him to launch Laughing Man Coffee and support farming communities
articles.body: A meeting in Ethiopia in 2009 changed how actor Hugh Jackman viewed coffee, inspiring him to launch Laughing Man Coffee and support farming communities through healthcare, housing, education and livelihood programmes. In 2009, Hollywood actor Hugh Jackman travelled to Ethiopia with humanitarian organisation World Vision and met a 27-year-old coffee farmer named Dukale, whose determination to support his family despite difficult circumstances left a lasting impression on him. The encounter eventually inspired Jackman to establish Laughing Man Coffee and the Laughing Man Foundation, turning his interest in coffee into an effort to support farming communities. According to World Vision and the foundation’s official website, the initiative has since supported programmes involving healthcare, safe housing, scholarships and community development.The story began in Ethiopia’s Yirgacheffe region, widely associated with the country’s coffee-growing tradition. Jackman and his then wife, Deborra-Lee Furness, visited the area to learn about community development initiatives supported by World Vision. During the trip, they met Dukale, a young farmer working to improve his family’s circumstances through coffee cultivation.The meeting that changed Jackman’s perspectiveJackman was already passionate about coffee, but his meeting with Dukale helped him understand the challenges faced by small-scale farmers who grow the beans consumed around the world.According to World Vision, Dukale worked long hours on his farm while facing obstacles that limited his ability to expand his business. Access to better markets and fair prices were also a major concern. His family faced everyday difficulties, including gathering firewood, which placed additional demands on their time and affected their opportunities to pursue education and other activities.Despite these challenges, Dukale remained determined to create a better future for his family. Jackman recognised a familiar ambition in the farmer’s efforts: the desire to work hard, support loved ones and provide children with opportunities that might otherwise remain out of reach.The encounter prompted Jackman to consider how consumers could support the people who produce the coffee they drink. Rather than limiting his response to a charitable donation, he began exploring whether a commercial venture could help connect farmers with customers while supporting their livelihoods.How Laughing Man Coffee was bornTwo years after the Ethiopia visit, Jackman launched Laughing Man Coffee in 2011. The venture was designed to combine speciality coffee with a social mission, giving consumers a way to support programmes benefiting farming communities.The business was built around the idea that coffee could create value beyond the product itself. By developing a market for speciality coffee, the venture sought to help farmers reach consumers and benefit from greater commercial opportunities.Jackman worked with entrepreneur David Steingard, who was developing a speciality coffee business. The partnership helped turn the idea into a commercial enterprise. According to a 2011 report by BroadwayWorld, Laughing Man Worldwide was established to support entrepreneurs and promote the idea that commerce and community development could work together. Laughing Man Coffee & Tea was the first business developed under that model.At its launch, the company said 100% of the profits from its stake in the businesses it created would go to charity. Its wider mission focused on education, community development and supporting entrepreneurs.The business later expanded its reach through retail and packaged coffee products. However, the brand’s commercial arrangements have evolved, so its original profit-sharing model should not automatically be taken to mean that every current sale or revenue stream is donated in full.From coffee sales to safer homes and scholarshipsThe Laughing Man Foundation grew out of the promise Jackman made after meeting Dukale and his family. Its work focuses on helping coffee-farming communities overcome barriers that prevent families from improving their living conditions and building more secure futures.The foundation’s official website says it has provided healthcare, safe homes, scholarships, business training and emergency support in Ethiopia, Peru and Colombia.These programmes address needs that extend beyond the farm. Access to healthcare can help families deal with medical challenges, while safer housing can improve everyday living conditions. Scholarships and educational support can give young people opportunities to continue their studies, and business training can help individuals develop skills to strengthen their livelihoods.The foundation’s approach reflects the lesson Jackman drew from his meeting with Dukale: a farmer’s ability to improve his family’s circumstances depends on more than the quality of the coffee he produces. Access to markets, education, healthcare and basic infrastructure can also influence whether a family has a realistic opportunity to move beyond poverty.The organisation says it is expanding its support through partnerships with other foundations, non-governmental organisations and companies, including initiatives in New York City and elsewhere.Coffee is one of the world’s most widely traded agricultural products, but the people who grow it do not always have equal access to the value generated along the supply chain. Small-scale farmers can face challenges involving production costs, market access, fluctuating prices and limited resources.Fair-trade initiatives seek to address some of these concerns by improving trading conditions and supporting more sustainable livelihoods. Their impact depends on how programmes are structured and implemented, and a single business cannot resolve every challenge facing coffee-producing communities.You use AI every day. articles.title: Zelenskyy sounds alarm as Russia hits Ukraine’s energy sites despite Trump’s ceasefire announcement
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday accused Russia of continuing to attack Ukraine’s energy facilities despite US President Donald Trump’s
articles.body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday accused Russia of continuing to attack Ukraine’s energy facilities despite US President Donald Trump’s announcement about energy infrastructure ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv. Zelenskyy said Russian strikes had hit a power plant in Kharkiv, a gas production facility and a civilian gas station.Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had learnt about the purported agreement through media reports. He said Russia had not publicly confirmed its acceptance of the proposal.“We support it, but I have not heard approval of this proposal from the Russian side,” Zelenskyy said.Referring to Trump's announcement on Truth Social, Zelenskyy said Ukraine had been “horribly surprised" by the strikes that followed the US president's post.“It was clear that Putin does not read Truth Social,” Zelenskyy said.Trump had announced the purported agreement on Sunday, saying it took effect immediately but providing few details about its terms or implementation."Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it! Thank you for your attention to this matter," Trump said in a post on Truth Social.Zelenskyy says Ukraine ready to honour ceasefireIn a separate statement on Monday, Zelenskyy reiterated Ukraine's willingness to support the ceasefire and said Kyiv was awaiting details from Washington. He stressed that Russia must also agree to the arrangement for it to work.In a post on X, Zelenskyy said, "Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well. We are awaiting details from the American side. For our part, Ukraine always FULLY supports steps toward de-escalation, the protection of lives, and the decisions needed to end the war and guarantee lasting peace."Zelenskyy also said Ukraine was prepared to stop attacking Russian oil refineries if Moscow halted strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure. He urged Trump to press the Kremlin to agree to the arrangement.Warning of a possible escalation if Russia refused to comply, Zelenskyy said Ukraine would respond if Moscow did not agree to an energy ceasefire during the winter."We are waiting for the details of the conversation between the Americans and the Russians, and we are waiting to see what specific steps the Americans are ready to take," he said."This energy ceasefire can work, and it can become a major step toward ending the war."Trump had previously announced a similar arrangement that did not result in a lasting halt to attacks. In a social media post on September 14, he said Russia and Ukraine had agreed “not to hit” each other's energy infrastructure, but provided no details about the proposal.Russia has repeatedly targeted Ukraine's energy infrastructure during the war, disrupting electricity, heating and water supplies for civilians. Ukrainian officials have described the strategy as “weaponizing winter” and fear Moscow could intensify attacks as temperatures fall.Ukraine has also targeted Russian energy facilities, including oil refineries deep inside Russian territory.EU chief doubts Russia will honour truceEuropean Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas on Monday welcomed the prospect of a halt to energy strikes, particularly with winter approaching, but questioned whether Russia would respect the arrangement.“We haven’t yet seen that also Russia will stick to it,” Kallas said at a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Luxembourg.“Personally, I would also welcome that the ceasefire would include people not being killed, not only energy.”Kallas also pushed back against Trump's comments on Saturday that Ukraine should elect a new president. She said elections should not be held during the war without a ceasefire.Estonian foreign minister Margus Tsahkna questioned Trump's reported deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel amid high fuel prices in the US.Tsahkna said he did not believe the deal “is actually going to change anything” in terms of fuel prices, adding that it was ”much more connected to the domestic situation in the U.S."Ukrainian and European officials have criticised the reported diesel arrangement, arguing that it could help fund Russia's war effort.Zelenskyy says elections impossible during warZelenskyy said holding elections in Ukraine remained impossible while Russian attacks continued, including strikes carried out during the day and night.“Under such circumstances, it’s impossible to hold elections,” he said.However, he added that he would be ready to work towards holding elections if Ukraine secured a full ceasefire lasting at least 60 days.His remarks came after Trump said on Saturday that it was time for Ukraine to have a new president and criticised Zelenskyy for not doing enough to end the war.Russian drone attack kills three in Kharkiv regionA Russian drone attack on the village of Pisochyn in the Kharkiv district on Sunday evening killed three people and injured nine others, including children, according to the Kharkiv Regional Prosecutor's Office.Investigators said the attack took place at around 7.25pm in a densely populated area near apartment buildings and grocery stores. It also sparked a fire.Ukraine's Air Force said its air defences had shot down or suppressed 89 of 121 Russian drones launched overnight into Monday. The attack also involved a Kh-59 guided air-to-surface missile and included 76 jet-powered Shahed-type drones.Strikes were recorded at 15 locations, while debris from downed drones fell at four sites.Russia's Defence Ministry said its air defences had intercepted 151 Ukrainian drones overnight over Russian regions, Crimea, which Moscow illegally annexed in 2014, and the waters of the Black Sea.In a separate statement, the ministry said Russian forces had carried out overnight drone strikes on unspecified Ukrainian port infrastructure and a bulk carrier heading to Odesa with military cargo on board.You use AI every day. articles.title: Democrats aim to elect 100 women to House as party eyes control of Congress in US midterms
articles.summary: As Democrats look to wrest control of Congress from Republicans in the November midterm elections, the party is also aiming for a historic milestone:
articles.body: As Democrats look to wrest control of Congress from Republicans in the November midterm elections, the party is also aiming for a historic milestone: electing at least 100 women to the House of Representatives.With women candidates contesting several key races that could determine control of the House, Democratic leaders believe they could have as many as 113 women in their ranks next year if the party performs strongly in competitive districts, The New York Times reported.“I’m incredibly confident that we will pass that 100 mark,” Representative Teresa Leger Fernández of New Mexico, chairwoman of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, told the newspaper.Democrats currently have 97 women in the House, accounting for around 45 per cent of their caucus. Reaching 100 would set a new record for the party. In the 1980s, women made up less than 5 per cent of House Democrats.Women candidates central to Democrats’ midterm strategyDemocrats have placed women candidates at the centre of their campaign to regain the House majority. According to The New York Times, 18 of the 40 Democrats in the party’s “Red to Blue” programme, which backs candidates challenging Republicans in competitive districts, are women.More than a dozen women are contesting closely fought races, while several are considered strong contenders to flip Republican-held seats.Fernández said women would help Democrats win a majority both by winning congressional seats and by voting for Democratic candidates.“Women are going to give Democrats the majority in two ways,” she said, adding that women and Latinos had been among the groups hardest hit by Republican policies.If Democrats regain control of the House, women lawmakers are expected to push issues including childcare and elder care.Republicans lag in women’s representationRepublicans currently have 32 women in the House, including two nonvoting delegates, accounting for around 15 per cent of their members. Their numbers could decline further if vulnerable Republican women lose their seats in November.Political observers say greater female representation could influence debates on gender discrimination, sexual harassment and violence against women.Kelly Dittmar, a political science professor at Rutgers University, told The New York Times that increased representation could also change how political institutions function.For Democrats, the midterms offer an opportunity to challenge Republican control while increasing women’s representation in Congress. Whether they reach the 100-member milestone will depend on the outcome of competitive races in November.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Is daylight saving time happening this year? Will this be the last time for the US?
articles.summary: Yes, daylight saving time is happening in the United States in 2026, with clocks scheduled to fall back by one hour on Sunday, November 1.
articles.body: Yes, daylight saving time is happening in the United States in 2026, with clocks scheduled to fall back by one hour on Sunday, November 1. The annual change will bring an end to daylight saving time for the year, as most of the country returns to standard time for the autumn and winter months.Under the current federal rules, daylight saving time begins on the second Sunday in March and ends on the first Sunday in November. In 2026, it began on March 8 and will end on November 1. The change will apply to all states that observe daylight saving time. Hawaii and most of Arizona do not follow the practice.When do clocks fall back in 2026?Clocks will be turned back at 2 am local time on November 1, moving from 2 am to 1 am. This means people in areas observing the change will effectively gain an extra hour.Most smartphones, computers and internet-connected devices will update automatically. However, some clocks and household appliances may need to be adjusted manually.The end of daylight saving time will also affect daylight hours. Sunrise and sunset will occur about an hour earlier by the clock, bringing more daylight to the morning and less to the late afternoon and evening.Is the US ending daylight saving time permanently?The United States continues to observe daylight saving time despite recurring efforts to eliminate the twice-yearly clock changes. Under the existing federal schedule, clocks must still be changed in March and November in states that observe the practice.Supporters of making daylight saving time permanent argue that longer evening daylight would benefit businesses, recreation and everyday life. Opponents have raised concerns about darker winter mornings and the potential effects on commuters, schoolchildren and early risers.Any change to the current nationwide schedule would require the necessary legal action. Until then, the November 1 clock change remains scheduled. The House passed the Sunshine Protection Act by 308-117 in July, but the Senate has not advanced it. President Donald Trump has renewed his calls to make daylight saving time permanent.When will daylight saving time return in 2027?Daylight saving time is scheduled to begin again on Sunday, March 14, 2027. At 2 am local time, clocks will move forward by one hour, provided the current rules remain in effect.Until then, states that observe daylight saving time will remain on standard time through the winter.The winter solstice, the shortest day of the year in the Northern Hemisphere, will occur on December 21, 2026. Daylight hours will gradually increase after that point, ahead of the return of daylight saving time in March.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: For 11 years, Danielle Steel quietly funded a San Francisco homeless outreach team; four trucks carried food, clothing and sleeping bags on rounds designed to support 300 people at a time
articles.summary: For 11 years, bestselling author Danielle Steel quietly funded an outreach operation that brought practical supplies directly to people experiencing
articles.body: For 11 years, bestselling author Danielle Steel quietly funded an outreach operation that brought practical supplies directly to people experiencing homelessness in San Francisco. Every three weeks, a 12-person team set out in four trucks carrying warm clothing, rain gear, sleeping bags, tarps, hygiene products and packaged food that did not need cooking or refrigeration. The rounds were designed to support about 300 people at a time, for 10 months of each year, as per her website. Steel described the work as a “mission of love” on her foundation’s website, where she explained that the programme was run anonymously and paid for by her. The effort was organised through Yo! Angel!, a foundation she established to support street outreach. Its work has since been suspended because the cost became prohibitive.A personal commitmentSteel’s philanthropic work has long been shaped by her son, Nick Traina, who died in 1997. Her website says she established two foundations in his memory, each with a distinct purpose. The Nick Traina Foundation supports organisations working on mental health, suicide prevention and child abuse prevention, while Yo! Angel! was created to organise and fund direct assistance for unhoused people in San Francisco.The outreach work recognised that homelessness and mental illness can overlap. Steel wrote that many people the team met on the streets were living with mental health challenges, and that the programme was designed to bring useful supplies directly to them. Rather than operating from a fixed location, the team travelled through the city to reach people where they were.The effort was a personal commitment as well as a charitable programme. Steel says, on her foundation’s website, that Yo! Angel! was fully funded by her and that the team worked anonymously for all 11 years. The focus was not public recognition, but making sure people had items that could help them manage the difficult conditions of street life.Four trucks, a practical missionThe scale of each round was substantial. A 12-person team used four trucks to carry supplies intended for roughly 300 people. The outreach took place every three weeks, 10 months of the year, creating a recurring routine rather than a one-off distribution.The supplies were selected for everyday use. Warm clothing and rain gear could offer protection from changing weather, while sleeping bags and tarps provided basic shelter materials. The team also brought practical items such as flashlights, umbrellas, eating utensils and water bottles.Hygiene supplies were included as well, along with packaged food intended to last three weeks. Steel specified that the food did not need to be cooked or refrigerated, an important detail for people without reliable access to a kitchen or safe food storage.The mix of items suggests an effort to respond to several immediate needs at once. A water bottle, flashlight or set of utensils may seem ordinary, but these tools can be hard to replace when someone is living outdoors. Supplying them directly allowed the team to reach people who might not be able to travel to a service centre or store their belongings safely.Outreach built on consistencyThe programme’s schedule mattered. By going out every three weeks, the team returned regularly instead of distributing supplies only during a particular season or public campaign. That rhythm gave the work continuity and allowed the team to provide essentials repeatedly over the course of the year.Steel’s account does not describe the outreach as a substitute for housing, healthcare or long-term support. It was a direct response to immediate needs, focused on useful supplies for people living on the streets. The team’s regular visits offered practical help, while the broader challenge of homelessness remained.The project also reflects a model of philanthropy that can be less visible than a large public event. The work took place on the streets, away from galas and cameras, and Steel says it remained anonymous throughout its operation. The foundation’s website describes the effort as a “true mission of love,” a phrase that captures its personal and hands-on character.Sharing the experience in a bookSteel later wrote A Gift of Hope about the outreach work and the people the team encountered. On her foundation’s website, she says she hopes the book will open readers’ eyes and hearts to the difficult circumstances faced by people experiencing homelessness.Writing about the work extended the project’s reach beyond the streets where the team operated. The book gave Steel a way to describe what she had seen and to encourage readers to look more closely at homelessness in their own communities. It also preserved the story of an effort that had been conducted quietly for more than a decade.Steel has said she lent her voice to the issue because homelessness is a serious problem in cities. Her account does not frame the work as a simple solution. Instead, it presents the outreach as one way to meet immediate needs and to make people’s circumstances harder to ignore.Why the programme pausedYo! Angel!’s outreach has been suspended for the time being. Steel says the cost of running it became prohibitive, and the foundation did not have the fundraising drives that support the Nick Traina Foundation’s work. The pause marks the end of the regular truck rounds, though it does not erase the years of assistance already provided.The suspension also points to the financial demands of sustained direct service. Four trucks, a 12-person team and supplies for hundreds of people every three weeks required significant resources. Steel had funded the programme herself, but eventually the expense became too great to continue in the same way.Her website remains a record of what the outreach involved: a carefully organised effort to bring food, clothing and practical tools to people living on San Francisco’s streets. It also shows how one person’s philanthropy can support consistent, hands-on work for years, even when it remains outside the public eye.A quiet legacy of careFor 11 years, Steel’s team carried more than supplies. It carried the promise that people living outdoors would be met with practical help on a recurring basis. The programme’s reach was measured not in headlines, but in four trucks arriving with items people could use.The work has now paused, but its story remains part of Steel’s wider charitable legacy. Through Yo! Angel!, she supported people facing homelessness with food, warm clothing, sleeping bags and other essentials, while also drawing attention to the challenges they face.In a city where homelessness is a visible and persistent issue, the outreach offered a simple form of care: show up, bring useful things and return again. articles.title: Frank Lloyd Wright’s only built planetarium stopped functioning in 2004 and saw limited use for more than two decades; after a multiphase restoration, the 1960 space has reopened to the public
articles.summary: For more than two decades, the stars inside a remarkable Frank Lloyd Wright creation had largely gone dark.
articles.body: For more than two decades, the stars inside a remarkable Frank Lloyd Wright creation had largely gone dark. Now, the universe is once again unfolding beneath its distinctive dome. Florida Southern College in Lakeland, Florida, has reopened Wright’s only built planetarium following a multiphase restoration, bringing a rare piece of architectural and scientific history back into active use, states an online report by West Orlando News.A Wright design unlike any otherAccording to West Orlando News, located inside the Polk Science Building, the planetarium is part of Florida Southern College’s extraordinary collection of 13 structures designed by Wright. The campus holds the largest single-site collection of Wright architecture anywhere in the world.The report states that the planetarium occupies a special place within that collection. Wright had spent decades considering the idea of designing a planetarium before incorporating one into his plans for the science building. His broader vision extended beyond architecture itself, imagining educational spaces that could serve students as well as the wider community.Construction took place between 1954 and 1958, with the first planetarium show presented on April 7, 1960. The space subsequently became an important part of Florida Southern’s astronomy programme, hosting students, school groups and members of the public, states the report by West Orlando News.From dormant space to modern planetariumThe original projection system eventually stopped functioning in 2004. Although the space continued to see occasional use, the planetarium was largely inactive while restoration plans took shape. The revival unfolded in several stages. Exterior work received support from the State of Florida and private funding, while interior restoration was backed by federal Save America’s Treasures funding and private donors.The latest phase has transformed the restored interior into a functioning contemporary planetarium. A new COSM projection system and Bowen sound system now provide the technology needed to once again turn the space into an immersive environment for exploring the cosmos.Importantly, the restoration has sought to preserve the architectural character of Wright’s original design rather than turning the historic space into a generic modern venue.Exploring the universe once againThe reopened planetarium will offer public programmes four days a week, with shows scheduled on Tuesdays, Thursdays, Saturdays and Sundays, informs the online report. Six programmes will rotate through the calendar, covering subjects ranging from the solar system and Mars exploration to exoplanets and the search for life beyond Earth.It is also reported that individual presentations run for approximately 20 to 32 minutes, while the complete visitor experience is expected to last between 60 and 90 minutes. Visitors will also receive an introduction to the history and architectural significance of the planetarium before the featured programme begins. Admission is priced at $20 per person, with a reduced rate of $15 per person for families and groups of four or more, adds the online report.A space designed for the publicThe reopening restores more than a building; it revives Wright’s idea of education extending beyond the traditional classroom. The planetarium will support Florida Southern students and faculty while welcoming school field trips, community organisations and other groups, claims the report.Images Courtesy: istock and West Orlando NewsYou use AI every day. articles.title: A cargo ship to Europe, with a spare cabin
articles.summary: Every summer, as Arctic ice thins, a few container ships sail from China to Europe over the top of the world.
articles.body: Every summer, as Arctic ice thins, a few container ships sail from China to Europe over the top of the world. The trip takes about 20 days, half the 40 it takes via Suez. This year, Chinese carriers began running it as a scheduled service, with the Dubai Tower leaving Ningbo in mid-August for Felixstowe, Hamburg and Gdynia.Tourists do visit the Arctic, but on cruise ships built for the purpose, with expedition jackets and a lecture on polar bears. Nobody, as far as we could find, sells a berth on a working container ship making the same crossing. It is an odd gap, considering how many people will pay good money to be somewhere remote.The idea is simple. A handful of passengers travel on a real cargo vessel, and not in a separate deck with better curtains. They bunk with the crew, eat in the mess and, if they like, help out with light duties. The ship is carrying batteries and solar panels, not guests. The passenger is cargo of a rather unusual kind.The timetable would be just as honest. Arrival depends on ice and weather, so a ship due on the 7th may turn up on the 6th or the 9th. Most holidaymakers would baulk at that. Some would find it the best part. In an age when an app tells you the food will reach you in 11 minutes, a journey that refuses to name an arrival date has its own appeal.There is evidence such travellers exist. Freighter travel is a small but loyal trade, with cabins going for around 150 euros a day including meals, and popular routes selling out months ahead. Fewer than 3,000 people a year travel this way worldwide, and big lines like Maersk have stopped carrying passengers altogether. Demand is steady, supply is shrinking, and the Arctic version does not yet exist.The catches are real. The navigation window runs only from late July to early November. Insurers will need convincing. Cargo ships usually carry 12 passengers or fewer, and no doctor, so age and fitness limits would apply. And cargo will always come first, so a route or a date can change at short notice.None of that is fatal. A shipping line does not have to build anything. It needs a spare cabin, an insurance policy and the nerve to print "arrival date approximate" in the brochure. Indians, who have spent generations on overnight trains that arrive when they arrive, may be better placed than most to enjoy it.The first ticket should not be hard to sell.You use AI every day. articles.title: Hyundai Bayon launch date out: Design, cabin images & more
articles.summary: Hyundai Motor India has unveiled the India-spec Bayon, ahead of its launch in the country on October 26, 2026.
articles.body: Hyundai Motor India has unveiled the India-spec Bayon, ahead of its launch in the country on October 26, 2026. Bookings for the new SUV are already open through Hyundai dealerships and the company's official website. The Bayon will be positioned as an Intelligent Utility Vehicle, with a major focus on connected technology, artificial intelligence and software-based features.The Bayon gets a sculpted bonnet, new front fascia and a full-width LED light bar, rectangular headlamp clusters mounted lower down and chunky bumper trim. The sides feature sharp Z-shaped lines, black wheel arch cladding and geometric multi-spoke alloy wheels. At the rear, a full-width LED taillight strip mirrors the front design, while a dark skid plate and floating roof rails complete the SUV's rugged look.Hyundai Bayon: PowertrainPowering the Hyundai Bayon is a four-cylinder 1.5-litre MPi petrol engine developing 115 hp and 144 Nm of torque. The engine is rated at 84.4kW and 14.7kgm of torque. Customers will be able to choose between a 6-speed manual transmission and CVT.The Hyundai Bayon will be launched in India on October 26, 2026. Bookings are currently open for an amount of INR 11,000 through Hyundai dealerships and the company's official website. Deliveries are scheduled to begin during the festive season, with detailed delivery timelines to be announced at launch.Hyundai Bayon: Loaded with techOne of the key highlights of the India-spec Bayon is Hyundai Motor India's first Generative AI Voice Assistant. The system combines Intelligence by Perplexity with Voice AI powered by SoundHound AI. It is designed to understand conversational requests rather than depending only on a fixed set of voice commands.For example, occupants can ask the system to prepare a travel itinerary, provide real-time weather information, suggest hotels or restaurants, recommend nearby shopping destinations, or provide sports coverage, scores and insights.The SUV also gets Hyundai's Connected Car Navigation Cockpit (ccNC), which is accelerated by NVIDIA. The system brings together online navigation, a personalised control panel, split-screen functionality and smartphone-like quick controls into a single interface.Another major technology feature is Vehicle Controller Over-the-Air (C-OTA) capability. The Bayon has up to 19 controllers that can receive OTA updates, allowing software enhancements and feature updates to be carried out remotely without requiring a visit to a dealership. Hyundai says this can also help with safety, security and reducing maintenance requirements.Hyundai Bayon: Cabin and featuresInside, the Bayon gets dual 62.5 cm (12.3-inch + 12.3-inch) curved panoramic displays. The two screens form a unified digital cockpit and display driving information, navigation, entertainment and connected functions.The SUV also gets Hyundai Bluelink with more than 70 connected features. These include remote start/stop, connected vehicle information, remote vehicle controls, smartphone and smartwatch connectivity, location and navigation services, and safety and security features.Hyundai has also focused on making the technology more accessible to Indian customers. The infotainment and instrument cluster interface supports 10 regional and two international languages. In addition, the SUV gets more than 500 embedded voice commands in English, Hindi, Hinglish, Tamil, Bengali and Telugu. These commands can be used for several in-car functions without an internet connection.

articles.title: US agents raid lawmaker Ilhan Omar's home as part of immigration fraud probe
articles.summary: Federal agents raided the Washington-area home of Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar early Monday as part of an ongoing federal investigation into her
articles.body: Federal agents raided the Washington-area home of Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar early Monday as part of an ongoing federal investigation into her immigration paperwork.Homeland Security Investigations searched through a warrant authorised by a court and obtained by the Department of Justice, a DOJ spokesperson told Fox News Digital.“Today in the Washington, DC area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice,” the spokesperson said, adding that the action was part of an ongoing federal investigation.The probe reportedly focuses on immigration documents filled out by Omar’s late father when she was a child. The Somali-born lawmaker, who represents Minnesota, has previously faced allegations surrounding her immigration history, including claims that she married her brother to help him enter the United States.Omar has strongly dismissed the allegations, describing them as “absurd and offensive.”The raid marks an escalation in the investigation, which border czar Tom Homan publicly acknowledged in September.Homan declined to provide details about the case at the time but warned that “no one’s above the law”. He also declined to rule out the possibility of revoking Omar’s US citizenship.Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin had also indicated that the investigation extended beyond questions surrounding Omar’s 2009 marriage, saying that removal proceedings could follow if wrongdoing was established.The Department of Justice and Omar’s office had not immediately responded to requests for comment, according to reports.Omar, a prominent member of the progressive group known as the Squad, has been among President Donald Trump’s most vocal critics in Congress and has frequently drawn attacks from the president.The investigation comes as Minnesota faces increased scrutiny from the Trump administration over immigration enforcement and a sprawling Medicaid fraud scandal. Federal prosecutors have warned that the alleged fraud could involve billions of dollars.The state, which is home to the largest Somali community in the US, has also been at the centre of tensions over federal immigration operations following the fatal shootings of US citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal immigration agents in January.The incidents sparked widespread protests and criticism, including from some Republicans, putting further pressure on the administration’s immigration policies ahead of the November midterm elections.Omar married political consultant Tim Mynett in March 2020, following the finalisation of her divorce from Ahmed Hirsi, with whom she has three children.You use AI every day. articles.title: Suspected IED explodes in J&K's Poonch; security heightened
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: An explosion, suspected to have been caused by an improvised explosive device (IED), was heard in a forward village along the Line of Control
articles.body: NEW DELHI: An explosion, suspected to have been caused by an improvised explosive device (IED), was heard in a forward village along the Line of Control (LoC) in the Krishna Ghati sector of Jammu and Kashmir’s Poonch district on Monday, prompting heightened security measures, officials said.An explosion by a suspected improvised explosive device (IED) was heard in a forward village along the Line of Control in the Krishna Ghati sector of Jammu and Kashmir's Poonch district on Monday, triggering heightened security measures, officials said.The powerful blast reportedly took place in the Satwal-Naki area near the zero line while a group of people was moving along the Pakistani side of the LoC, officials said as per a PTI report.Casualties were reported, but the exact number of people killed or injured was not immediately known, they added.Officials said it was unclear whether the group comprised suspected terrorists attempting to cross the LoC or Pakistani security personnel patrolling the area. The circumstances leading to the explosion were yet to be established.Security heightened Following the blast, security forces sounded an alert across the sector and stepped up vigilance along the LoC to assess the situation and prevent any potential security breach, officials said.In a separate incident, Indian Army troops detected two rusted landmines near the border fence in the Basoni area of the Mendhar sector on Monday.The landmines were spotted during track construction at 8.25 am and 12.10 pm, respectively, officials said. Both devices were subsequently destroyed by Army experts in controlled explosions.Around a dozen landmines have been detected and defused by the Army in the area over the past week.Forward areas along the LoC are dotted with landmines as part of an anti-infiltration system. However, heavy rainfall can sometimes wash the mines away, causing them to surface in areas where they could pose a potential risk.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Assam chief minister Himanta Biswa Sarma slammed Congress amid the ongoing INDIA bloc protest against SIR and 'vote chori', while directly
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Assam chief minister Himanta Biswa Sarma slammed Congress amid the ongoing INDIA bloc protest against SIR and 'vote chori', while directly challenging Rahul that he's ready to contest on ballot paper if Congress govt's in Kerala, Telangana, Karnataka resign.Addressing a press conference in Guwahati, he hit out at Rahul and the Congress and challenged, "I am ready to contest on the ballot paper if Rahul Gandhi and Congress are ready for their governments' resignations. The Kerala, Karnataka and Telangana governments must resign because those governments were also formed through 'vote chori' under Gyanesh Kumar.""Today, the Congress doesn't even have enough people to stage a protest in Delhi. They had to hire and bring people in from Assam, gathering them from all over the country... I am ready," Himanta further said.Further continuing his jab, he added, "Make the proposal; I want to set a standard where I resign as an MP and then launch a movement."He also defended the SIR saying, "The SIR is needed in India. Assam, West Bengal and Jharkhand's demography changed due to huge illegal immigration. articles.title: From a 23-day hunger strike to a Connaught Place sprint: Meet Neha Bora
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: By 2.30pm on Sunday, a crowd had begun to gather near RK Ashram Marg Metro station.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: By 2.30pm on Sunday, a crowd had begun to gather near RK Ashram Marg Metro station. Neha Bora had called for the agitation to go on, and her supporters answered. So did the police, in large numbers.Within minutes, the gathering turned into a chase. Bora broke into a run towards Connaught Place, and protesters streamed after her, past the barricades. At 2.51pm she announced on social media that they had made it to CP. Police caught up soon after, and by about 3pm she was in custody. Others were carried to waiting buses, struggling as they went.The aim was to reach Jantar Mantar and press for the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The woman leading the dash is the 29-year-old president of the All India Students’ Association (AISA), who had ended a 23-day hunger strike at the same spot only recently.The bus, in her tellingAfter her detention, Bora posted a video on X describing the police bus as a vehicle with four cramped cells and no room to breathe. She alleged that women were packed into a small compartment and that male protesters were abused and kicked. Police have not responded to these claims in the reports available.Many Jantar MantarsThe run was the second act of a defiant weekend. After Saturday’s detentions, she told supporters that another part of Delhi would become Jantar Mantar the next day. She had also asked those who couldn’t reach the protest site to regroup near Dilli Haat. They gathered in the INA area, where police detained her and others.A soldier’s daughterNeha grew up in Khatima in Uttarakhand, in a family that moved from city to city with her father’s Army postings. She has lived in Delhi for nearly 12 years, but the hills remain her reference point. She pushes back on the stereotype of the soft-spoken hill woman, saying that strength is what has kept her going.When home disagreesHer father, who is still in the Army, and the rest of the family do not share her politics and are uneasy about her activism. She says the difference has not shaken her convictions.Theatre first, politics laterNeha's activism did not begin with slogans. At Delhi University, she acted in plays on social issues, and that stage work widened her worldview. She later joined a group that took such causes to the streets. She calls the journey “an organic progression”, something that was never planned.Shaped by anti-CAA stirThe 2019 protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act were a turning point. She says being on the ground changed many who were there, her included.The scholarBora is a PhD scholar at Jawaharlal Nehru University, working in theatre and performance studies. It is a fitting field for someone who has spent years learning how to hold an audience, whether in a hall or at a barricade.The fastShe was one of three JNU scholars who fasted with activist Sonam Wangchuk at Jantar Mantar. After 23 days without food, she was left weak, though her fever had subsided. She spoke to TOI about her life and politics on Thursday, on her way back to the protest site.The grievanceNeha Bora traces the agitation to policy rather than any single event. articles.title: Archaeologists uncovered a 200-year-old shipwreck buried in Canadian sand dunes; clues point to a vessel lost in 1812
articles.summary: Archaeologists excavated a shipwreck on Sable Island in May 2025 that researchers believe may be the Swift, a sloop that ran aground in 1812.
articles.body: Archaeologists excavated a shipwreck on Sable Island in May 2025 that researchers believe may be the Swift, a sloop that ran aground in 1812. If confirmed, the identification would establish a rare link between a shipwreck site on the island and a documented wreck from before the 20th century.According to Parks Canada, the Swift was one of three ships that ran aground on September 27, 1812, while travelling from Bermuda to Newfoundland. The site first came to light in February 2024, when a winter storm exposed parts of the wreck, including copper sheathing bearing a British Royal Navy broad arrow and a stamp dated January 1810. During the later excavation, archaeologists uncovered larger sections of the vessel buried in the sand along the island’s North Beach.How a storm exposed the 200-year-old shipwreck on Sable IslandThe site first came to attention during routine monitoring in February 2024, when a winter storm exposed a small piece of wreckage on Sable Island. Staff also found a section of copper sheathing bearing a British Royal Navy broad arrow and an Admiralty stamp dated January 1810, from Portsmouth.Archaeologists recognised the broad arrow as a mark used by the Royal Navy to identify its property. Historical records identify HMS Barbadoes as the only known British naval ship to have wrecked on the island’s northeast side. The frigate had also undergone a refit at Portsmouth in 1810, linking the sheathing to the vessel.What connects the shipwreck to the 1812 maritime disasterParks Canada archaeologists have determined the two large sections uncovered at the site belong to the same vessel, which may be the Swift. Several clues support this possibility. The wreck appears to be that of a small, single-deck vessel with one mast. Fragments associated with HMS Barbadoes were also found nearby, pointing to a possible link with the same wreck event.The site’s location matches historical maps showing where the Swift ran aground. The wood also appears to be Bermuda cedar, which is consistent with the possibility that the vessel was a Bermuda sloop travelling from Bermuda to Newfoundland. Together, these clues support the identification, although Parks Canada has yet to confirm that the wreck is the Swift. All three ships were lost in the September 1812 incident.Two excavations uncovered larger sections of the shipwreck on Sable IslandThe excavation took place during two trips to Sable Island, in May 2024 and May 2025. During the first visit, archaeologists documented the exposed wreck and uncovered a larger section buried deep beneath a dune. Uncovering the section buried beneath the dune required more time and the use of mechanical tools. When the team returned in May 2025, they uncovered another large section of the wreck that was more complete than expected.The vessel lay beneath loose, uniform sand with no distinct soil layers, so archaeologists used sandbags to stabilise the excavation banks. They removed most of the sand with a skid steer before switching to hand tools to avoid damaging the wreck. The team recorded the vessel’s structure and visible features to scale before the shifting sands covered the wreck once more.How the shipwreck is being studied and protected for future researchAfter exposing the wreck, the team documented its timbers, visible features, and nails. They also recorded its position using a survey instrument and drone, and collected wood and copper samples for analysis. Studying the wood can help researchers identify the species and determine whether different pieces came from the same vessel. In some cases, tree-ring analysis can also help establish the wood’s age and origin.Once the work was complete, the team reburied the wreck in sand to protect it from oxygen, which can rust metal and encourage fungi that decay wood. Parks Canada will continue to monitor the site, as shifting sands may expose more artefacts. Researchers will also analyse their findings and investigate questions about the ships and their crews over time.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Cops detain anti-SIR protesters, assault journalists in Bengaluru
articles.summary: BENGALURU: On a day Karnataka chief minister DK Shivakumar and home minister Priyank Kharge protested against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of
articles.body: BENGALURU: On a day Karnataka chief minister DK Shivakumar and home minister Priyank Kharge protested against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and police action against protesters in Delhi, police in Bengaluru detained dozens of protesters and assaulted photojournalists covering the action on Monday.Personnel in plain clothes were also seen acting aggressively towards protesters and journalists outside SJP college — opposite the chief electoral officer (CEO) office — which is within 1 km of Freedom Park, the designated protest site in Bengaluru.The protesters, including students, lawyers, activists and academics, had gathered to march to the chief electoral officer’s office to demand that SIR be scrapped and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resign.However, police began detaining them before the march could begin, according to activist group My Vote, My Right. The group said police confiscated placards and detained people before they could begin the march.Protesters were pushed, dragged and forcibly taken away in buses. Police personnel were also seen beating young protesters and pulling at the clothes of women protesters, the group said. Advocate Vinay Sreenivasa told TOI: “They used force and detained several of us and released us at the CAR (city armed reserve) grounds. Clifton Rozario, the national general secretary of All India Lawyers Association for Justice, was assaulted.”Among others detained and later released were activist and author Aakar Patel, members of AILAJ, members of My Vote, My Right, a coalition of over 40 civil society organisations, including trade unions, women’s groups, and human rights organisations. Photojournalists covering the protest and police action were also targeted. One photojournalist was beaten by four police personnel, while three other journalists were manhandled, which protesters also confirmed.A photojournalist covering the incident said police assaulted a group of students and objected when journalists tried to record the action. When he continued filming, an officer told him to delete the footage.“One person came and said, delete it,” he recounted. As journalists continued recording the detention of women protesters, police personnel objected. A photojournalist was threatened and beaten, while another was pushed to the ground after police grabbed his phone and threw it aside. He was also pulled by the collar, pushed from behind and hit on the leg, according to his account. An officer threatened to put him in jail.The journalists were attempting to document police personnel pushing and pulling women protesters. The photojournalist said there were few women police personnel present as male officers handled the protesters.The protest was organised to condemn the police action against anti-SIR protesters in Delhi, where activists, lawyers, students and journalists have been detained during demonstrations demanding the scrapping of SIR and Kumar’s resignation.My Vote, My Right said it had been demanding the withdrawal of SIR since Oct 2025, arguing that the exercise could lead to mass disenfranchisement. It cited the deletion of names from electoral rolls and an Indian Express investigation into objections raised by two of the three Election Commissioners as reasons for continuing protests.The detentions in Bengaluru drew criticism on social media, including from people who said their family members had been taken away.“My daughter and her friend who went to join anti-SIR protests in Bangalore have just been detained. Why is this happening in a Congress-ruled state even when the young step out in support of your cause? Please respond,” Arpita Das, associate professor of writing at Ashoka University, posted on X, tagging Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi and Kharge.Prateek Waghre, sharing a video of the police action, questioned the Karnataka govt’s response to the protesters. “For all your posturing against RSS, your police is acting like it is administered by an RSS offshoot political party,” he posted, tagging Kharge.The activists demanded that SIR be scrapped and Kumar resign. They also said they had intended to submit a memorandum to the chief electoral officer. Police had not issued a response to the allegations of assault and manhandling at the time of writing.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'Absolute faith in judiciary': Congress rejects Keralam party unit's post on CJI Surya Kant
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Congress on Monday expressed disagreement with a social media post by its Keralam unit on Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, with party MP
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Congress on Monday expressed disagreement with a social media post by its Keralam unit on Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, with party MP and spokesperson Pawan Khera saying the Congress has "absolute faith in judiciary."The party also removed the individual responsible for the post from their position.Also Read | ‘Dear Surya Kant ... ’: Congress Keralam unit’s post asking CJI to 'resign' draws BJP fireThe post, which has since been deleted, addressed the CJI by name and called on him to "resign." It was in response to the CJI's remark, as quoted by PTI, that law and order did not fall within his domain. The CJI was referring to the unprecedented security restrictions imposed by Delhi Police amid ongoing protests in the national capital demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar."We completely disagree with this position, whoever has done it. It is completely incorrect. We have absolute faith in the judiciary of this country and respect the highest court. That is exactly why we went to the doorstep of the highest court and knocked on its door because of the confidence we have in the judiciary," Khera told ANI.Meanwhile, Keralam Congress president Sunny Joseph said the post was published without its knowledge."The person responsible for an objectionable post against Supreme Court Chief Justice Surya Kant on the party’s official X account has been removed from the position. The post was published without the knowledge, consent or consultation of the KPCC leadership. The KPCC will examine the circumstances under which the post was published. The Congress party has no disagreement with the impartiality of the judiciary. Social media posts expressing views contrary to this position do not reflect the stand of the KPCC leadership."The BJP, meanwhile, criticised the Congress, accusing the opposition party of being “anarchist.”“Anarchist Congress! This is a big insult to Constitution of India! Congress is threatening Chief Justice of India! Congress thinks Gandhi Vadra Parivar is above the Constitution! Congress hates Indian democracy & independent Constitution bodies!” BJP national spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari posted on X.BJP MP Nishikant Dubey wrote: "After the President, Vice President, Prime Minister, and Chief Election Commissioner, now Maharaja @RahuGandhi ji has demanded the resignation of the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court as well. According to sources, after this resignation, Rahul Gandhi ji will become Prime Minister, Sharjeel Imam President, Abhijeet Deepke Vice President, Priyanka Gandhi ji Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, and Khalistani Pannu Chief Election Commissioner. Soros will be India's ambassador in America."This came after leaders of the Congress-led opposition INDIA bloc moved the Supreme Court against the Election Commission (EC), naming the poll body, Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar and Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi as respondents.The petition was filed after the Chief Justice of India declined the opposition’s request for a meeting to submit a representation on alleged “vote chori” (vote theft) by the EC for the ruling BJP. CJI Kant later explained, “I received a letter yesterday (Sunday) regarding a meeting request, and I responded to it last night, outlining the reasons why I will be unable to meet.”“The Supreme Court's doors are open to everyone. Any petition from any common citizen or member of an elected body is welcome. Every Indian citizen has the right to approach the court, and we will hear their concerns and grant whatever is due under the law,” he added.SCBA condemns Keralam Congress postMeanwhile, the Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA) condemned the Keralam Congress' post, saying such remarks "undermine the judiciary and amount to interference in the administration of justice."“Statements of this nature belittle the institution of the judiciary and amount to an attempt to interfere with the administration of justice,” the SCBA said. It emphasised that every individual has the right to approach the courts and seek legal remedies, while urging its members and others to uphold the “dignity and decorum” of the Supreme Court of India.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.summary: West Bengal clears 11 new border police outposts near Bangladesh and Bhutan, creating 209 posts to boost patrolling, intelligence and faster response this year.
articles.body: Kolkata: Bengal govt has approved 11 new police outposts in border areas near Bangladesh and Bhutan to improve security and reduce cross-border crime.A total of 209 posts have been created for these outposts. Each outpost will have one sub-inspector, three assistant sub-inspectors and 15 constables.Seven outposts will be set up in Alipurduar along the Bhutan border: Hatipota under Samuktala PS, Pasakha under Jaigaon, Lanka Para and Bandapani under Birpara, Hantapara under Madarihat, Sankosh under Kumargram and Chuapara under Kalchini PS.Three outposts will be set up in Malda along the Bangladesh border: Lanagola and Pakua Hat under Bamangola. articles.title: Mamdani directs NYPD to review use-of-force policy after officer involved in teen’s fatal shooting retires
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has ordered the New York Police Department (NYPD) to conduct its first comprehensive review of use-of-force policies in
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has ordered the New York Police Department (NYPD) to conduct its first comprehensive review of use-of-force policies in a decade and announced an additional $2.6 million in funding for independent police oversight.The move comes after an officer involved in the fatal shooting of 19-year-old Win Rozario, who was experiencing a mental health crisis, was allowed to retire before facing an internal disciplinary trial. The New York Post reported that the decision angered Rozario's family.“When the government uses force against a New Yorker, the standard for accountability must be at its highest. Every New Yorker deserves to know that force will be used lawfully, carefully and only when necessary,” Mamdani said in a statement.Rozario was shot dead in March 2024 after police responded to a 911 call at his home in Ozone Park, Queens.Body camera footage showed officers firing at him after he charged at them with scissors, despite his mother and brother pleading with police not to shoot. Officers had used Tasers against him twice before opening fire.Two officers, Matthew Cianfrocco and Salvatore Alongi, fired their weapons at Rozario, who later died in hospital.New York Attorney General Letitia James decided in December 2025 not to bring criminal charges against the officers, although they remained subject to an internal disciplinary process.One of the officers was allowed to retire last week before the disciplinary trial could take place, prompting fresh concerns over police accountability.“We have an obligation to Win’s family and to every New Yorker who calls for help in a moment of crisis,” Mamdani said.The mayor said the review would examine whether the department's policies adequately guide officers on the use of force and whether changes are needed.The process will also include community engagement and assess the training officers receive when responding to critical incidents.Mamdani's administration also announced a $2.6 million increase in funding for the Office of the Inspector General for the NYPD, an independent body that examines the department's policies and operations. The additional funding is expected to triple the office's current headcount, strengthening its capacity to investigate police practices and improve oversight.Other measures include a new notification system to help ensure disciplinary proceedings are completed before officers retire.The NYPD will also formalise notifications to the state when officers retire while facing disciplinary charges, with the aim of preventing them from joining other law enforcement agencies in New York.The department will also maintain compliance with state reporting requirements for police-involved deaths and formalise the sharing of information with families and the public after critical incidents.Final reports from the NYPD's Force Investigation Division will be made available to families or their representatives upon request.The administration said the measures are intended to strengthen transparency, ensure serious allegations are addressed and improve public trust when police use of force results in death or serious injury.You use AI every day.
